This game takes a lot of aspects of the first game and builds on them. Having the heroes fighting on the field is an interesting new mechanic. I've enjoyed the game quite a bit. So why am I giving it a negative review? I feel like I got tricked. The first game had a shop to unlock permanent upgrades. I kept pushing forward thinking "Maybe it'll open up if I unlock all the characters. No? Okay, maybe if I go really far into endless mode... still no? WTF!?" Come to find out after some digging around, there -is- no permanent upgrade shop anymore. Without that, I don't really have any reason to keep facing challenges in this game. I've got all the characters, and I don't do achievement-hunting. I want to feel a sense of progress, a sense of reward for facing and overcoming challenges. This game doesn't have that anymore, and it's extremely disappointing. I'm sure that's fine for some people, but I never got into that sort of Dark Souls mentality of playing something difficult just to play something difficult.

Mage and Monsters II” isn’t a roguelike autobattler — it’s Dragon’s Lair (1983) disguised as one. You pick a hero, juggle gold versus upgrades, and push as far as possible — but that’s it. On the surface it looks like an autobattler, but it doesn’t feel like one. A true autobattler is about reacting in real time, countering enemy builds, and winning through clever unit composition and adaptation. This game strips all of that away. You just pick one upgrade path (“chunk”) and mindlessly buy whatever fits it. There’s no strategy, no improvisation, there is nothing. Every run is the same 30 preset waves. The supposed “roguelike randomness” is a façade. The actual gameplay loop is pure trial and error: 1. Pick a hero 2. Push until you hit a wave you can’t beat 3. Die 4. Adjust your build order 5. Repeat until you memorize the “correct” sequence There is single optimal solution to every wave, and you’re just bashing your head against the wall to discover it. This is just a game about memorization. The "random" draft system is equally deceptive. You pick 1 of 3 units from a “random” pool, but the pool itself is so tiny (5–6 units total) that rerolling is meaningless. You’re effectively just paying an extra 2 gold to buy what you wanted anyway. Same goes for upgrades: dull numerical boosts like “+10% damage” or “+10% health.” Nothing creative, nothing exciting — just stats going up, and reroll being meaningless because you can pick whatever you want. And because of how scaling works (attack speed × base damage × attack speed again = cubic growth), the game actively punishes diverse armies. You’re forced to commit to one upgrade aspect if you want to survive. Variety is a trap. Meta progression? Nonexistent. You unlock a new hero by winning with another hero. After about ten runs, you’ve seen everything. No permanent upgrades, no unlockables, no evolving strategy — just a new round of memorization for each new hero you play. In reality, this isn’t a roguelike. It’s a deterministic memory game masquerading as one. You “win” by writing down the correct build order for every hero and difficulty, and executing it perfectly. Once solved, it’s dead. There’s no replay value, no tension, no creativity. The game feels like a tech demo, not a finished title. To actually become a game worth playing, it would need: - Real meta progression (permanent upgrades, meaningful unlocks) - True randomness and build diversity - Interesting, creative upgrades - Strategic freedom, not rigid solutions As it stands, it’s hollow. The only thing you can do for fun is test which hero gets furthest in endless mode — but even that feels empty, since the optimal build for each hero is basically predetermined. Yes, it’s an indie project. But it’s not complete. It feels like an early access prototype pretending to be a finished release.

The concept is there, but zero balance. The game is packaged like you get choices to how you level up, but most of the heroes and units are so incredibly underpowered and the balance is so bad that it makes many of heroes unplayable even on easier difficulties. The illusion of choice quickly fades when you realize that in every 30 wave run, there will be enemies mixed in that are impossible to work around unless you build an absolutely 100% specific way (almost impossible considering it's a rng game that all choices inevitably lead to failure). I've watched most of the players who tried when it came out disappear real quick because of this. It wouldn't be so bad if there were anything at all recovered from failed runs, but no. They skipped any and everything that would involve depth, strategy, and customization and left it as bare bones as possible, then instead of listening to the 2 dozen people who still stick around to play it, they just keep adding more broken characters and avoid making the actual game fair or rewarding. The original game offered more than the sequel. This game is the equivalent to Son of the Mask.

First of all, I really, really like the game! And I am so torn on whether to give it a positive or a negative review. The one negative thing that stands out to me is that it has no meta progression at all. Zero. Which is really strange for a game tagged as "action roguelike". And as different as the characters are, I feel like more often then not, every round is nigh identical to the last. Apart from that, the game is very enjoyable but I see no reason to sink a 100 hours or even 10 hours into the game. Which saddens me, because I really would've liked to.

Incredibly addicting auto battler! Build armies and observe if you can defeat your oponents. In between fights buy/upgrade your troops and hero, learn new spells (the only active element in a fight), rinse and repeat the loop. However don't spend all your gold in one round as the game rewards you with a nice interest bonus if you decide to keep the money and manage to win the next fight. With hundreds of sprites on screen many of the battles are certainly epic. Audiovisually it's pretty decent as well. Nothing to add really. Fun, simple, addicting. Doesn't overstay its welcome. Great buy for a few euro's. Recommended! Rating: 8.0/10

This is review coming from an avid enjoyer of the first Mage & Monsters game. Mage & Monsters 2 really added a lot more depth and quality of life to the auto battler system that already made the first game very enjoyable. • Heroes. Not only is there a much bigger roster of heroes, most of them actually fight in the battlefield now and have their own abilities/health rather than simply being more of a "perk" like the first game. They are practically your very own "boss" on your side and you can upgrade them indefinetely and make them really OP if you wish. That brings me to my next point. • Upgrades. The upgrade system is MUCH better compared to the first game. Not only can you upgrade army stats like the first game, you can now upgrade your Hero as stated before, as well as your spells INDEFINITELY. The first game had limitations on spell upgrades and the army upgrades went up in price dramatically, but now those army stat upgrades can be purchased as many times as you want at the regular price. This new upgrade system allows you freedom to many different playstyles. You can spend all your upgrades on making a really OP Hero, an insanely strong army, or incredibily OP spells, or any kind of mixture in between! • Army Upgrades. What I mentioned above were specifically the stat upgrades, but now each specific unit in the game has unique optional upgrades that give that unit a specific perk such as more evasion, critical chance, stun chance, etc. It adds another level of customization and playstyle. • Unit Bonuses. The game now rewards you by having a diverse army with additional "perks" if you have many different "types" of units - Demons, Humans, Elves, and Beasts. You unlock all the bonuses if you buy one of each type of army unit. Many of these bonuses are very powerful like evasion chance for elves and spawning a skeleton upon death for demons. These bonuses can also be shared by different types of units if you buy and upgrade to "Share" those bonuses. I've unlocked all the achievements in both games and Mage & Monsters 2 was much easier to unlock all the achievements. Thankfully the dev didn't require you to beat the game with each Hero at the hardest difficulty unlike the first game. I still did it with most heroes because I like the challenge, but the first game was FAR more brutal because you are way more limited in your strategy compared to this game as I've mentioned above. It's way easier to cheese especially with a lot of heroes. There is definitely some balancing that needs to be done however, some heroes are clearly much stronger than others. I do like that Effero from the first game is also one of the strongest heroes here like he was in Mage & Monsters 1. The last thing I will point out is that the Hero portraits for the new heroes are terrible... the first game had pretty good pixel art. This game kept the same cool portraits for the returning heroes, but all the new hero portraits look so bad and were clearly done by a different artist. Thankfully the in game sprites look pretty good as well as the army and enemy unit sprites. Anywy I've really enjoyed this game, and despite it being easier compared to the first game to unlock all the achievements it still provides a really good challenge which I love. Highly recommended.

Not enough to warrant double the price anyway. I feel like it doesn't do enough to improve on the formula of the original. If anything, the heroes undermine the army building. You can invest all your upgrades into building a single unkillable dragon-slaying tank of a unit and that's all it takes to win even on the hardest "Hell" difficulty.
